title: The brain: how we sense, notice and remember
source: DeepKids Combined. A DeepKids topic beyond the boards (the brain, nerves and reflexes, perception, attention, memory, sleep, feelings, and other minds), linking to the senses and body chapters of NCERT, Cambridge and NIOS. No textbook needed.
summary: A grown-up's brain weighs about as much as a 1.3 kg bag of rice, yet it uses a fifth of the body's energy. Your child learns that it is made of about 86 billion nerve cells called neurons, and that nerves carry messages to and from it. They test their reflexes and reaction time. They find their blind spot and try an illusion, which show that the brain makes a best guess of what we see. They measure their own forgetting, and find that practice after a gap, and sleep, make memories last. Last, they meet crows, octopuses and a slime mould with no brain that finds its way through a maze.
builds_on: Builds on Class 1 and 2 work on the senses and the body, and on Class 3 health (sleep, and feelings in the body). Class 5 goes further: the parts of the brain, how memory rebuilds the past, why we sleep, emotions, and the question of consciousness.
goals: By the end your child can explain that the brain is made of billions of neurons that pass electrical and chemical signals, and that nerves carry messages to and from it.
By the end your child can show a reflex and measure their own reaction time.
By the end your child can show, with the blind spot and illusions, that the brain builds what we see as a best guess.
By the end your child can explain why we miss things we are not paying attention to.
By the end your child can explain how practice and sleep turn short-term memories into long-term ones, using their own forgetting test.
By the end your child can describe how crows, octopuses, bees and a brainless slime mould sense, learn and solve problems.
subconcepts: the brain: where it is, what it weighs, how much energy it uses
nerves: messages from senses to brain, and brain to muscles
reflexes act before we decide, and reaction time
the brain builds what we see: the blind spot and illusions
attention: we notice what we focus on and miss much of the rest
practice strengthens connections, like a path in grass
feelings are made by brain and body together
what it feels like to be you (subjective experience)
other animals' minds: crows, octopuses, bees
thinking without a brain: single cells and slime moulds
words: brain
the organ in your head that controls the body and makes thoughts, feelings and memories
neuron
a nerve cell that passes messages using electricity and chemicals
synapse
the tiny gap where one neuron passes its message to the next
nerve
a bundle of long neurons that carries messages around the body
reflex
a quick action the body does without you deciding, like blinking
perception
the brain's way of making sense of what the senses send it
illusion
a picture or sight that makes the brain see something wrongly, like two equal lines that look different
attention
choosing what to notice and focusing on it
memory
what the brain keeps from the past
mind
our thoughts, feelings and awareness: what it's like to be us

days.title: Where are you?
days.goal: Wonder where 'you' are, start a time journal, and hear the story.

steps.title: Point to yourself
steps.do: Ask your child: 'Point to yourself.' Most children point to their chest. Ask: 'Is that where you are? Where do your thoughts happen?' Many will now point to their head. Ask: 'If you lost a finger, would you still be you? What part could you not lose and still be you?' Don't settle it. Say: 'People have argued about this for thousands of years. This week we learn about the organ that has a lot to do with it: the brain.'

steps.title: Story: The Path Through the Long Grass
steps.do: Read the story aloud (Story tab). It is about Ayesha, a girl learning the flute. Ask the story questions. Don't explain what the path has to do with the flute yet. Your child will find out this week.

steps.title: Thought clouds
steps.do: Sit together quietly, eyes closed, for one minute. Say: 'Just watch your thoughts come and go. Don't chase them.' Then your child draws a cloud for each thought they noticed, with a picture or a word inside (a sound, a worry, a food, a song). Ask: 'Did you choose those thoughts, or did they just come?' Keep the drawing. You'll do this again on Day 8.

steps.title: Start the time journal
steps.do: Start Activity a1, a time journal. Every evening this week your child writes three things that happened, one feeling, and sticks in one small thing, like a ticket or a drawing.

need: a small notebook for the time journal

days.title: 86 billion messengers
days.goal: Find out what the brain is made of, and start a forgetting test.

steps.title: How heavy is a brain?
steps.do: Fill a plastic bag with 1.3 kg of rice or ragi flour (weigh it). Your child holds it. Say: 'A grown-up's brain weighs about this much. That is only about 2 parts in 100 of the body's weight. But it uses about one-fifth of the energy from your food, even when you're asleep.' Ask: 'Why would something so small need so much food?' (It is always working. Billions of cells are sending messages, all the time.)

steps.title: Counting the neurons
steps.do: Say: 'The brain is made of nerve cells called neurons. Each one has branches that receive messages and a long tail that sends them on. The message travels along a neuron as a tiny electric pulse. Between one neuron and the next is a tiny gap called a synapse. Chemicals carry the message across it.' Draw one together. Then tell voice v1: books said humans had 100 billion neurons, but nobody had counted. Suzana Herculano-Houzel, a Brazilian scientist, found a way to count them. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: The neuron squeeze
steps.do: Do Activity a2. The family holds hands in a line and passes a squeeze, like neurons passing a message. Time how fast it travels.

steps.title: Start the forgetting test
steps.do: Start Experiment e2: your child learns 10 made-up word pairs. You'll test them over the next days.

need: a plastic bag and 1.3 kg of atta or rice
the word-pair list from Experiment e2

days.title: Nerves, reflexes and reaction time
days.goal: Feel reflexes that act before you think, and measure your reaction time.

steps.title: Forgetting test: 1 day later
steps.do: Without looking at the list, test the word pairs from Experiment e2. Say the first word, and your child gives its partner. Write down the score. Don't show the answers.

steps.title: Reflexes and the ruler drop
steps.do: Do Experiment e1: the knee-jerk, the blink and the ruler drop.

steps.title: The roads of the body
steps.do: Draw a body outline with the brain and the spinal cord, a thick bundle of nerves running down inside the backbone. Draw nerves branching out to the fingers and toes. Say: 'Your senses send messages along nerves to the brain. The brain sends messages back to the muscles. A reflex is a short-cut. The message goes to the spinal cord and straight back to the muscle. So you pull your hand off a hot pan before you even feel the pain.' Ask: 'Why is that useful?' (It is faster, so you get hurt less.)

steps.title: One toe, one eyebrow
steps.do: Try this: move only your right big toe. Now only your left little finger. Now only one eyebrow. Ask: 'Which was hardest? Why?' (We use some movements far more than others, so the brain's connections to those muscles are stronger.)

days.title: Your brain is guessing
days.goal: Catch the brain filling in and being fooled.

steps.title: Time journal: yesterday
steps.do: Your child reads yesterday's time journal entry. Ask: 'What do you remember about yesterday that you didn't write down? Is your memory of it the same as mine?' Compare one moment you both remember.

steps.title: Find your blind spot
steps.do: Do Experiment e3, the blind-spot card. Your child guesses first, then tries it. Ask afterwards: 'When the dot vanished, what did you see in its place?' (Just white card. The brain filled the gap with the white around it.) 'Why don't you notice your blind spot every day?'

steps.title: Illusions
steps.do: Draw two lines, each exactly 10 cm long, one above the other. At both ends of the top line, draw a V that opens away from the line, like this: >——<. At both ends of the bottom line, draw arrowheads: <——>. Ask: 'Which line is longer?' Most people say the top one. Measure them. They are the same. Ask: 'Now that you know, does the top one still look longer?' (Yes.) Say: 'Your brain does not show you the world like a camera. It makes a best guess from what your eyes send, using what it has seen before. Usually the guess is right. When it is fooled, we call it an illusion.' Ask: 'Then how can we be sure what is real?' (We check. We measure, we ask others, we test.)

steps.title: What does red look like to you?
steps.do: Hold up something red. Ask: 'What colour is this? How do you know that the red you see is the same as the red I see?' Let your child think. Say: 'Nobody can get inside your head and see your red. What it is like to be you, to taste payasam or to feel happy, is called subjective experience. Scientists still don't know how a brain makes it.' Then your child paints how today feels, using only colours and shapes, with no people or things. Ask: 'Would someone else know what you felt by looking?'

need: a white card and a black pen

days.title: The spotlight of attention
days.goal: Find out how attention works, and what we miss.

steps.title: Forgetting test: 3 days later
steps.do: Test the word pairs from Experiment e2 again and write the score. Then show the list once. This is the review. Ask: 'Did you remember more or fewer than on Day 3?'

steps.title: The invisible gorilla
steps.do: Tell voice v4. Then, if you can, watch the short 'selective attention test' video by Daniel Simons on YouTube. Your child counts how many times the players in white pass the ball. Don't say what else to look for. Afterwards ask: 'How many passes? Did you see anything unusual?' Many people miss a person in a gorilla suit who walks right through. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: What changed?
steps.do: Your child looks around the room for 30 seconds, then leaves it. You change three small things: move a tumbler, turn a photo, take a pen off the table. Your child comes back and tries to find all three. Then swap. Ask: 'Why was it so hard, when it was right in front of you?' (The brain does not store every detail. It keeps the main picture and fills in the rest.)

steps.title: Worksheet: brain basics (core)
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1. Your child explains each answer aloud before marking it.

need: a phone or computer to watch the video (optional)

days.title: Memory paths, and sleep
days.goal: Learn how memories are made, kept and lost, and how sleep helps.

steps.title: Forgetting test results
steps.do: Do the last test of Experiment e2. Draw a graph: test number along the bottom, score up the side. Ask: 'When did you forget fastest?' (Usually soon after learning.) 'Did the review help?'

steps.title: Short-term and long-term memory
steps.do: Say seven digits once, like 4 9 1 7 3 8 2. Your child repeats them straight away (usually easy). Talk about something else for a minute, then ask for them again (often lost). Say: 'That was short-term memory. It holds a few things for a short time. Long-term memory keeps things for years. Each time you practise, the connections between the same neurons get stronger, like the path in the story.' Then say: 'While you sleep, the brain replays the day, and memories get stronger. That is how Ayesha woke up able to play.' Ask: 'So is it better to sleep or to stay up late studying?'

steps.title: Calkins' pairs game
steps.do: Tell voice v2, about Mary Whiton Calkins, who invented the word-pairs test you have been doing. Then play. Make 8 pairs of a colour and a number ('blue 7, red 3'). Say them once, then test. Next, make a new list, and this time make a silly picture for each pair ('a blue whale with 7 legs'). Ask: 'Which way worked better?' (Pictures usually help, because they link the new thing to things you already know.) Ask the voice question.

steps.title: The week, told backwards
steps.do: Your child reads their time journal from Day 1 to today. Then they tell the week backwards, from today to Day 1. Ask: 'What did you remember only because you wrote it down? Which days are already fading?' Say: 'Writing is how people keep memories outside their heads. History is memory that was written down.'

need: the forgetting-test scores and graph paper

days.title: Other minds: feelings, animals and brainless thinkers
days.goal: Explore feelings, other animals' minds, and whether thinking needs a brain.

steps.title: Feelings in the brain and body
steps.do: Ask: 'Where in your body did you feel your last big feeling?' (Many people feel fear in the tummy and anger in the face.) Say: 'Feelings are made by the brain and the body together. Your brain notices your fast heart and tight tummy, and what is happening around you. Then it decides: scared, or excited. That is why scared and excited can feel almost the same.' Ask: 'Have you ever felt both at once?'

steps.title: Clever animals
steps.do: Tell three true animal stories. Say: 'New Caledonian crows bend twigs and even wire into hooks, to pull food out of holes. An octopus has about 500 million neurons, and two-thirds of them are in its arms. So each arm can touch, taste and explore partly on its own. Bumblebees can learn to roll a little ball to get sugar water. In one experiment, they kept rolling balls when there was no reward at all, as if playing.' Ask: 'What do you think it is like to be an octopus?' Say: 'Octopuses feel and think, but nobody knows yet what it is like from the inside.'

steps.title: Thinking without a brain?
steps.do: Tell voice v3. Say: 'J.C. Bose showed that plants send electrical signals when touched or hurt. A hundred years later, Toshiyuki Nakagaki put a slime mould in a maze. It has no brain and no neurons, but it found the shortest way to the food. Sensing, deciding and remembering began in single cells, long before brains. Brains came much later and made it faster. Some scientists say the word thinking should be kept for animals with nerves.' Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Worksheet: apply it (stretch)
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2. Let your child use the forgetting graph and the time journal.

need: pictures of a crow, an octopus and a bee if you have them

days.title: Brain Detectives: game and teach it back
days.goal: Put it together, play, and teach it back.

steps.title: Thought clouds again
steps.do: Repeat the thought clouds from Day 1: one minute of quiet watching, then draw the clouds. Compare with the Day 1 drawing. Ask: 'Were there more thoughts, or fewer? Was it easier to watch them? Are you your thoughts, or the one watching them?' There is no right answer.

steps.title: Brain Detectives
steps.do: Play the card game g1. For each card, the player must also say how they know.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3 (challenge). Discuss the written answers: there are good arguments on more than one side.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child shows a family member the blind spot and the ruler drop. Then they explain how memories are made, using the path in the story. Ask the check questions. Ask what surprised them most.

need: the blind-spot card and a ruler

sections.p: The brain is made of nerve cells called ____ .
The tiny gap where one neuron passes a message to the next is called a…
A reflex is…
opts: a quick action your body does without you deciding

sections.p: Match each to its job.
pairs: the main cable down the back
makes sense of messages and decides

sections.p: About how much of the body's energy does the brain use?
On the blind-spot card, the dot vanished at one point. Why?
opts: the eye has a spot with no light sensors, and the brain fills in the gap

sections.p: Many people who count passes in the ball video miss the gorilla walking through. What does this show?
opts: we notice only what we pay attention to
the gorilla was too small to see

sections.p: You knew the two lines were equal, but one still looked longer. What does that tell you about seeing?
In the 'What changed?' game, three small things in the room were changed. Why was it hard to spot them?
Short-term or long-term memory?
items: a phone number you just heard
what someone said a second ago

sections.p: In the forgetting test, you learned 10 made-up word pairs and were tested on several days. When did you forget fastest?
What helps a memory last?
opts: practising it again after a gap, and sleeping

sections.p: During ____ , the brain replays and strengthens the day's memories.
Think of the path in the story. Use it to explain why practising a little every day works better than practising a lot once.
Match the animal to its clever trick.
pairs: most of its neurons are in its arms
finds the shortest path through a maze, with no brain

sections.p: Sort these. Do scientists know this for sure, or is it still unknown?
items: octopuses have neurons in their arms
what it feels like to be a bee
what a slime mould's sensing feels like from inside
the brain uses a lot of energy

sections.p: Do you think a bee can feel happy? What evidence would help you decide?
Arjun and his sister Meenakshi do the ruler drop. Arjun catches the ruler at the 10 cm mark. Meenakshi catches it at the 20 cm mark. Who reacted faster?
opts: they reacted at the same speed

sections.p: Books said the human brain has 100 billion neurons. Then Suzana Herculano-Houzel, a Brazilian scientist, really counted them and found about 86 billion. What does this show about the old number?
Your brain makes a best guess of what you see. What is the problem with this?
opts: they can fool us, as in illusions and the gorilla video
they make us slower than a computer at everything

sections.p: Brain fact or myth?
items: we only use 10% of our brains
the brain builds what we see

sections.p: If your brain is always guessing, how could you check whether a memory is true?
Could a robot ever feel happy, or only act happy? How would we tell the difference?

Mary Calkins, an American scientist, did all the work for a Harvard PhD in 1895. Harvard refused her the degree because she was a woman. Later she was offered a degree from its women's college instead, and she said no. What would you have done, and why?
Nobody else can feel what it is like to be you. This inside experience is called ____ experience.

experiments.title: Reflexes and the ruler drop
experiments.question: Which actions happen without deciding, and how fast can we react when we do decide?
steps: Knee-jerk: your child sits on a table edge with legs hanging freely. Gently tap just below the kneecap with the side of your hand. Watch the lower leg kick. Ask: 'Did you decide to kick?'
Blink: hold a clear plastic file folder in front of your child's face. Gently toss a cotton ball at it. Do they blink, even though they know it can't touch them?

Ruler drop: hold a 30 cm ruler upright. The 0 cm end hangs between your child's open thumb and finger, not touching. Without warning, let go. They catch it as fast as they can. Read the number where they caught it.
Do the ruler drop 5 times and write each number. Then swap roles.
Try once with eyes closed. Say 'now' as you let go, so your child reacts to hearing instead of seeing.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will you be able to stop your leg kicking? How far will the ruler fall before you catch it?'
experiments.observe: The leg kicks and the eyes blink without your child deciding. In the ruler drop, most children catch it between 10 and 25 cm. Scores often get better with practice.
experiments.why: The knee-jerk and the blink are reflexes. The message goes from the sense to the spinal cord or the base of the brain, and straight back to the muscle. It does not wait for you to decide. The ruler drop is a reaction. Your eye sees the ruler move, the message goes to the brain, the brain decides, and it sends a message to your fingers. The further the ruler falls, the longer that took. A fall of 15 cm takes about one-sixth of a second. Messages in neurons are fast, but not instant.
experiments.safety: Tap the knee gently with the side of the hand only. Use only a soft cotton ball for the blink test, never anything hard.

experiments.title: The forgetting test
experiments.question: How fast do we forget, and does reviewing help?
need: the 10 word pairs below, written on a card
steps: Write 10 pairs of made-up words, for example: bim–tolo, zak–mepu, raf–siku, dov–lati, kep–yuno, mib–rasa, tuz–polo, gan–weki, lor–famu, vix–dobe.
Your child studies the list for 5 minutes, saying each pair aloud.
Test after 10 minutes: say the first word, your child says the partner. Write the score out of 10.
Test again on Day 3 (1 day later) without showing the list.
Test on Day 5 (3 days later), then show the list once to review.
Test once more on Day 6. Draw a graph of all the scores.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'How many will you remember tomorrow? In three days?'
experiments.observe: Most children remember many pairs at first, forget a lot by the next day, and forget more slowly after that. The review usually brings the score back up and makes it last longer.
experiments.why: In 1885, Hermann Ebbinghaus tested himself with nonsense syllables and found the 'forgetting curve': we forget fastest soon after learning, then more slowly. Each time we review after a gap, the memory gets stronger and fades more slowly. This is called spaced practice, and it works for spellings, tables and music. Made-up words are used so that nobody has an advantage from already knowing them.
experiments.time: 15 min, then 5 min on four later days

experiments.title: Find your blind spot
experiments.question: Can we see everything in front of us?
need: a white card about 15 cm long
steps: Draw a small X on the left of the card and a dot about 8 cm to its right.
Hold the card at arm's length. Close your left eye and look at the X with your right eye.
Keep looking at the X and slowly bring the card towards your face.
At one point, the dot vanishes! Keep going and it comes back.
Try drawing a line across the card through the dot. When the dot vanishes, what does the line look like where it was?
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will you see the dot the whole time?'
experiments.observe: The dot disappears when the card is about 25 to 30 cm from the face. The line looks unbroken, as if the brain painted it in.
experiments.why: At the back of each eye, the nerve to the brain leaves through one spot. That spot has no light sensors, so you are blind to a small patch. You never notice, because your other eye covers it. Even with one eye, your brain fills the gap with whatever is around it. So what you see is partly built by your brain. Octopuses have no blind spot, because their eyes are wired the other way round.

activities.title: Time journal
steps: Every evening, your child writes or draws three things that happened today.
They add one feeling from the day and what caused it.
They stick in one small thing: a ticket, a leaf, a sweet wrapper, a tiny drawing.
They write the time and the weather.
On Day 6, they read the whole week and tell it backwards.
activities.outcome: A week of memories kept outside the head, and a sense of how quickly memories fade without them.

activities.title: The neuron squeeze
steps: Everyone sits in a line holding hands. Each person is a neuron, and each pair of joined hands is a synapse.
The first person starts the timer and squeezes the next person's hand. Each person squeezes the next as soon as they feel it. The last person says 'Done!'.
Time it. Do it three times. Does it get faster with practice?
Now try passing the message by saying 'go' instead of squeezing. Faster or slower?
Ask: 'In the real body, messages travel up to about 100 metres a second in the fastest nerves. How long would our message take if each of us was a real neuron?' (A tiny fraction of a second.)
activities.outcome: A felt sense that messages travel from neuron to neuron, and that practice makes the chain faster.

project.title: My time journal and memory graph
steps: Keep the time journal every evening from Day 1 to Day 6.
Keep the forgetting-test scores and draw the graph on Day 6.
On Day 6, tell the story of the week backwards.
Make a small poster: 'How my memory works', with the forgetting graph, one page of the journal, and three tips for remembering (practise after a gap, make a picture or story, sleep).
Show it to the family on Day 8.
project.outcome: A week of real memory data about your own brain, and three tips you discovered yourself.

game.title: Brain Detectives
rules: Cut out and shuffle the cards. Put them face down.
Take turns: pick a card, read it aloud, and answer it. Say how you know.
A right answer with a reason wins the card.
'DO IT' cards are challenges: do them and win the card if the others agree.
Most cards at the end wins, but the winner must teach one card to everyone.

cards.front: What are the brain's message-carrying cells called?
About how many neurons are in a human brain?

cards.back: The tiny gap where one neuron passes its message to the next.
Blink when a cotton ball is tossed at a clear sheet, or do the knee-jerk.

cards.front: Why do you have a blind spot?
cards.back: Where the nerve leaves the eye there are no light sensors. The brain fills in the gap.
When the brain's best guess is fooled, like two equal lines that look different.

cards.front: Why do people watching the ball video miss the gorilla?
cards.back: They are paying attention to the passes, and we notice little outside what we focus on.

cards.front: Name the difference between short-term and long-term memory.
cards.back: Short-term memory holds a few things for a short time. Long-term memory keeps things for years, and practice makes it stronger.
The brain replays and strengthens the day's memories while we sleep.

cards.front: DO IT: remember these four in order: idli, kite, seven, blue. Another player checks after the next card.
cards.back: Use a silly picture to help.

cards.front: Where are most of an octopus's neurons?
cards.back: In its arms: about two-thirds of them.

cards.front: Which bird bends twigs into hooks?
What found the shortest path through a maze with no brain at all?
Who invented the word-pairs memory test and was refused a Harvard PhD?
True or false: we use only 10% of our brains.
cards.back: False: brain scans show we use all of it, just not all at once.

cards.front: DO IT: move only your left big toe.

cards.back: No: what it feels like to be you is subjective experience, and nobody knows how the brain makes it.

voices.idea: Textbooks long said the human brain has 100 billion neurons, but nobody had actually counted them. Herculano-Houzel found a way. She dissolved brain tissue into a liquid in which the centres of the cells float free. She mixed it well and counted them in tiny drops under a microscope. In 2009 she and her colleagues reported that an adult human brain has about 86 billion neurons.
voices.then: Her method was new and some scientists were doubtful at first, but it was checked and adopted by other labs.
voices.now: Her count is now widely used. She also found that the human brain is in many ways a scaled-up primate brain, not a strange exception, and that cooking food may have helped our ancestors afford such an energy-hungry organ. The 100 billion figure is still repeated in many books.
voices.ask: Everyone repeated '100 billion' for years without checking. What else might 'everybody knows' that nobody ever counted?

voices.idea: Calkins studied psychology at Harvard in the 1890s but, as a woman, was only allowed to attend as a guest. She invented the 'paired associates' method: learning pairs like a colour and a number and testing recall, which became one of the basic tools of memory research. She passed all the requirements for a Harvard PhD in 1895, and her examiners, including the famous William James, praised her highly.
voices.then: Harvard refused to give her the degree because she was a woman. It later offered her a degree from Radcliffe, its women's college, which she refused, as she had not studied there.
voices.now: She became the first woman president of the American Psychological Association (1905) and of the American Philosophical Association (1918). She never received the PhD. Her paired-associates method is still used.
voices.ask: Calkins refused the 'second-best' degree. Was that brave, stubborn, or both? What would you have done?

voices.who: Jagadish Chandra Bose (1858–1937), India, and Toshiyuki Nakagaki, Japan
voices.idea: From about 1900 to 1920, Bose built very sensitive instruments, like his crescograph. He showed that plants respond to touch, heat and chemicals with electrical signals, and that anaesthetics dull those responses, as they do in animals. In 2000, Nakagaki and colleagues put a slime mould in a maze, with food at two exits. A slime mould is one giant cell with no brain or neurons. It grew along the shortest route between the two foods.
voices.then: Bose's electrical measurements impressed scientists, but his claims that plants have something like feelings or a nervous system were widely doubted. Nakagaki's maze result was published in the journal Nature and was widely reported.
voices.now: Both findings are accepted. Plants do signal with electricity, and slime moulds do solve such problems. Scientists such as Michael Levin and Pamela Lyon show that sensing, deciding and remembering began in single cells, long before neurons. They call it basal cognition. Other scientists keep the words thinking and memory for animals with nerves. A slime mould is not a fungus or a bacterium. It is a living thing of its own kind.
voices.ask: A slime mould with no brain solved a maze. What did it have to sense and decide to do that?

voices.who: Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris, USA (1999)
voices.idea: In 1999 Simons and Chabris asked people to watch a short film of players passing basketballs and count the passes made by one team. Partway through, a person in a gorilla suit walks into the middle, thumps their chest and walks off. About half the viewers didn't notice the gorilla at all.
voices.then: The result surprised many people, including psychologists, and became one of the most famous experiments about attention, called 'inattentional blindness'.
voices.now: It has been repeated many times, in many versions. It shows that attention is limited and that we are often unaware of what we miss, and it matters for things like road safety (drivers who are busy with phones miss people crossing). How many people miss it depends on how hard the task is.
voices.ask: If you can miss a gorilla, what else might you be missing right now? How would you ever find out?

story.title: The Path Through the Long Grass
text: I am a path. I wasn't always one. Two years ago I was only grass, a field of tall grass behind the village in the hills of Wayanad, between Ayesha's house and her uncle Basheer's house on the other side. Then Ayesha started walking across me.

The first time she came, the grass stood up tall all around her, up to her shoulders, and she pushed through it, and behind her the grass sprang back up as if she had never been. The second time, a few blades stayed bent. The third time, a few more. You can't see a path being made, not on one day. But every time a foot comes the same way, a little more of the grass forgets how to stand up, and a little more of the earth gets pressed flat and hard.

By the end of that first summer, I was there. A thin brown line through the green, from Ayesha's back door to Basheer Mama's gate. I was quite proud of myself. Paths are made by walking, and I had been well walked.

Basheer Mama played the flute. Every evening when the light went gold, you could hear it from the field, a long, wavering sound like water running over stones. Ayesha wanted to play it more than she had ever wanted anything. So that winter he cut her a small flute from a piece of bamboo and showed her where to put her fingers, and every evening she came across me to learn.

She was very bad at it. I say that kindly. Paths are patient and we don't mind slowness. But at first the flute only made a sound like a kettle, or no sound at all, and Ayesha stamped her feet on me on the way home and said she would never learn.

Then she learned one note. Then three. Then Basheer Mama taught her a tune his own father used to play at weddings, a tune with a hard part in the middle where the fingers had to move quickly, lift, lift, press, lift, all in a row. And there she got stuck.

Every evening she tried the hard part, and every evening her fingers tangled. She came home across me muttering, "lift, lift, press, lift," in the dark. I could feel her feet getting heavier every night.
One evening in spring she came out of Basheer Mama's gate crying. She sat down right in the middle of me, in the dark, with the flute in her lap.
"My fingers won't remember," she said to nobody. "I do it right once, and then it's gone."
I wished I could tell her. I know about remembering. I'm made of it.

Here is the thing about a path. The first walk doesn't make it. The tenth doesn't. A path is made by walking the same way again and again, with a little time between, so the grass has time to bend and the earth has time to settle. And the strange part, the part nobody sees, is that a lot of the path-making happens when nobody is walking at all. At night. When the field is quiet and the dew comes down and the earth sinks into the shape the feet have pressed.
Ayesha sat on me for a long time. Then she wiped her face, got up and went home, and the light went off in her window, and she slept.
I lay in the dark with the shape of her footsteps on me, settling.

The next morning she didn't take the flute to Basheer Mama's. She sat on her back step in the early sun and, without really thinking, the way you hum when you're not trying, she put the flute to her lips and began the tune. She came to the hard part. And her fingers went lift, lift, press, lift, all in a row, as if they had always known.
She stopped. She stared at her fingers as if they belonged to somebody else.
Then she played it again. Lift, lift, press, lift.

Then she ran. She ran across me so fast her feet hardly touched, all the way to Basheer Mama's gate, shouting his name, and he came out with his tea in his hand, and she played it for him, the whole tune, hard part and all, standing at the gate in the morning light.
Basheer Mama didn't say anything for a while. Then he said, "Where did you learn that? Last night you couldn't do it."
"I don't know," said Ayesha. "I just woke up and it was there."
"Ah," said Basheer Mama, and he smiled, and drank his tea. "Then you learned it last night."
I didn't say anything. Paths can't. But I knew exactly what he meant.

Ayesha plays at weddings now. When she comes across me in the evenings I can feel how sure her feet are. The grass on either side of me is tall again, and there are other paths now in the field, thin new ones, where other children walk to other places.
Some of them are only a few blades bent. They'll get there.
story.epiphany: Memories are made like paths. The same connections between neurons are used again and again, with time in between, until they are strong. Much of the strengthening happens during sleep. The turn is Ayesha waking up able to play the hard part, and Basheer Mama's line: 'Then you learned it last night.'
ask: How did the path get made? Could one walk make it?
Why did Ayesha think her fingers wouldn't remember?
What did Basheer Mama mean when he said 'Then you learned it last night'?
What 'paths' are you making in your brain right now?

ideas.idea: Your brain does not record the world like a camera. It makes a best guess.
ideas.more: The blind spot, the illusion and the gorilla video show the brain filling in, guessing and leaving out. Usually the guess is good. That is why checking, measuring and asking others matter.

ideas.idea: Practice after a gap, and sleep, make memories last.
ideas.more: Each time you practise, the same neurons fire together and the connections between them get stronger. The forgetting graph and the story both show this.

ideas.idea: Minds are everywhere in nature, in many forms.
ideas.more: Crows make tools, octopuses explore with their arms, bees play, and a slime mould with no brain solves a maze. Some scientists keep the word thinking for animals with nerves. People have often decided too quickly that only minds like ours count.

unknowns: How does a brain, made of cells and chemicals, produce what it feels like to be you? This is sometimes called the 'hard problem', and nobody has solved it.
Exactly how and where memories are stored, and why some last a lifetime while others vanish, is still being worked out.
What is it like to be an insect, an octopus or a fish? The evidence that they feel keeps growing, but what their feelings are like from the inside is still unknown.
big: Are you your brain, or something more?
If your brain is always guessing, what is real?
How does something without a brain think?
If you forgot everything that ever happened to you, would you still be you?

challenge.hint: False. Brain scans show activity all over the brain. Different parts are busy at different times, and even in sleep much of it stays active. Nobody knows exactly where the myth came from. Ask: why do people like to believe we have a hidden 90%?

challenge.q: 'Some people are left-brained (logical) and some are right-brained (creative).'
challenge.hint: The two halves of the brain do have some different specialities (for most people, language is mostly on the left), but large studies have not found that people use one side more than the other. Logic and creativity use both. Ask: what's good and bad about sorting people into two kinds?

challenge.q: 'Humans have the biggest brains, so we're the smartest animals.'
challenge.hint: Elephants and sperm whales have much bigger brains than ours. Crows, with brains the size of a walnut, make tools. Herculano-Houzel found that the number of neurons, and where they are, matters more than size. And smart means different things for different lives. Ask: smart at what?

perspectives.view: Most of an octopus's neurons are in its arms, and each arm can touch, taste and explore partly on its own. Ask: what would it be like to think with your fingers?

perspectives.who: A meditating monk, or anyone practising dharana (attention) in yoga
perspectives.view: Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, an old Indian text, describe training attention to rest on one thing. Today scientists study whether this practice changes attention. The results look promising but are still argued about. Ask: can you train your attention?

When someone loses memories, are they still the same person? Families often say the person is still there in their laugh, their kindness, their songs. Ask: what part of a person is not in their memories?

check.q: What are neurons and how do they send messages?
check.a: Nerve cells that pass tiny electric pulses along themselves and chemicals across the gaps (synapses).

check.q: What is a reflex? Give an example.
check.a: A quick action the body does without you deciding, for example the knee-jerk or blinking.

check.q: What does the blind spot show about seeing?
check.a: The brain fills in gaps: what we see is partly built by the brain.

check.q: Why did many people miss the gorilla?
check.a: They were paying attention to the passes. We notice what we focus on and miss much of the rest.

check.q: What did your forgetting test show, and how can you remember better?
check.a: We forget fastest soon after learning. To remember better, practise again after a gap, make a picture, and sleep.

check.q: Name an animal with a surprising mind, and what it does.
check.a: For example, crows make hooks, octopuses explore with their arms, and bees roll balls.

check.q: A slime mould has no brain. What did it do in the maze, and does that count as thinking?
check.a: It sensed the food and grew along the shortest path to it. It sensed, decided and solved the maze, so it thinks in its own way. Some scientists keep the word thinking for animals with nerves.
